prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and its active forms, which enabled a new class of therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: B046 is the only candidate that all six of us ranked first, and that agreement rests on substance rather than momentum. It is a complete arc from hormone physiology (the secretion and processing of GLP-1, the identity of the active GLP-1(7-36) form, and its glucose-dependent insulinotropic action) to drugs that have changed the care of type 2 diabetes and obesity, with cardiovascular and renal benefit now shown in large outcome trials. Independent confirmation is overwhelming and the discovery is fully mature. The Holst, Drucker and Mojsov trio covers secretion physiology, receptor and tissue biology plus translation, and identification and synthesis of the active peptide. These are the contributions most clearly on the discovery side of the line.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Four credited names must be reduced to three, and the early GLP-1 literature has real priority disputes. Habener's group is not among the credited names, and Mojsov's credit relative to that group is contested. Leaving out Lotte Bjerre Knudsen can be read as favouring early physiology over the industrial design of long-acting analogues that put the drugs in patients. Part of the public impact comes from drug development, which the prize has treated inconsistently. A prize that looks like it rewards the product and omits its developers, or the reverse, would draw criticism either way.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks B040 second with June and Sadelain only, and suggests that Knudsen's liraglutide and semaglutide development could alternatively be recognised, since no GLP-1 configuration is uncontroversial.
responses.response: I agree that no GLP-1 configuration is uncontroversial. I would still keep the prize on the physiological discovery. Liraglutide and semaglutide are carefully engineered peptides, but the principle they exploit was already established by Holst, Drucker and Mojsov, and our criterion is discovery rather than product development. I would give Knudsen weight only if the committee wanted a two-part prize that pairs the physiology with a development achievement. I do not think that is needed, and it would use up scarce laureate slots. I agree with your CAR-T pair. I would keep Rosenberg out of it, because the CAR design and its clinical proof belong to June and Sadelain.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks B049 second and argues that a tool-based prize fits precedent, with Deisseroth plus Nagel and Hegemann as the core. He calls Knudsen the most dispensable credited name on B046.
responses.response: I agree on Knudsen. On optogenetics I accept that methods have been honoured before, but I am less comfortable with it than you are. The channelrhodopsin discovery is clearly physiology, but the most direct impact is on experimental practice, and clinical translation is only starting. Three of six credited people would also be left out, among them Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck, whose claims are real. That allocation problem is worse than anything in B046, so I keep B049 as an alternative and do not make it the lead.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks B040 second and B031 fourth, treats the Walter and Mori pair as clean and well confirmed, and doubts that Rosenberg's inclusion in CAR-T is secure.
responses.response: I share your view that Walter and Mori make the cleanest configuration on our list, and I rated it highly for that reason. It is a mechanism-first discovery that also bears on neurodegeneration, which I know from my own field. But it is not as urgent as B046, and its disease translation is still immature. On B040 I agree that Rosenberg's inclusion depends on how we frame the discovery. If the prize is for CAR design plus clinical proof, it should be June and Sadelain. Eshhar's absence from the credited names still leaves that configuration open to attribution criticism, which is why I place it as an alternative and not as a rival to B046.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius calls B046 a rare complete arc from hormone discovery to drug, but notes that Habener and others outside the credited list also matter, so the three-person limit forces contested choices.
responses.response: I agree, and this is the main uncertainty I carry. I would treat Habener as a limit of the supplied credit and not as grounds to hold back the prize. We can only award credited names, and the citation I propose is worded around the physiology of GLP-1 and its active forms so that it does not claim sole priority for any one group. I would resist a looser citation that pushes toward the whole field. If you think the committee should record Habener's role in its deliberations, I would support that.

responses.point: Perlmann places B015 (Hall and Schreiber for TOR) third and B031 fourth, avoids Sabatini for a leaner configuration, and sees the Mori and Walter list as a clean fair pair.
responses.response: I agree that leaving out Sabatini keeps the TOR configuration lean, but it also admits that the allocation among Hall, Schreiber and Sabatini is unsettled. Schreiber's rapamycin-FKBP12 chemistry may be judged a separate contribution from Hall's gene discovery. TOR is foundational, and its clinical reach beyond transplant and oncology is still unproven. I therefore would not move it ahead of B046, but I would keep it ahead of the HPV and cGAS-STING candidates in a later round if our first choice stalls.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a three-person B046 that excludes Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, or will want a second part for drug development.
How much weight the contested early GLP-1 priority record, including Habener's role and Mojsov's relative credit, should carry in the final allocation.
If B046 is somehow not decisive, whether B040 or B049 is the stronger fallback given the Eshhar gap in B040 and the six-name allocation problem in B049.
statement.conflict_note: Per my profile, I did a postdoctoral fellowship with Paul Greengard at Rockefeller, and the OpenAlex record lists about twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann on dopamine neurons, Nurr1 and autophagy (count not audited). Neither is a connection to any credited person on B046, B040 or B049, so no specific recusal issue is apparent from the provided profile. The Perlmann co-authorship is disclosed for transparency, because he is a fellow committee member.
